titre: The 1930 Convention Against Forced Labor Organized Its Own Postponement
accroche: Adopted in Geneva in 1930, the ILO convention against forced labor provided for its own transitional period, removed from the text 84 years later.
contenu_vulgarise:
Geneva, June 28, 1930. Meeting in its fourteenth session, the International Labour Conference adopts Convention No. 29 on forced labor, the first international text to define and combat this practice. Its Article 2 lays down a broad definition: forced or compulsory labor means all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself voluntarily. The convention excludes five categories from this scope: compulsory military service of a purely military character, the normal civic obligations of a fully self-governing country, prison labor carried out under public supervision, work required in cases of force majeure such as war, a calamity, or a famine, and minor communal services close to ordinary civic obligations.

## A Convention That Organized Its Own Postponement

The text adopted in 1930 does not stop at prohibiting and exempting, however. Its Articles 1, paragraphs 2 and 3, and 3 to 24, organize a transitional period during which certain members of the International Labour Organization may continue to use forced labor, under controlled conditions rather than an outright ban. In practice, these provisions target the colonial powers, which at the time made wide use of forced labor in their overseas territories, to build roads and railways or to exploit resources. The convention lays down a general principle of suppression within the shortest possible period, a phrase that leaves each state to judge how long that is.

## A Postponement That Lasts Eighty-Four Years

These transitional provisions, designed for limited use in time, are nevertheless repealed neither in the decades following decolonization nor during the twentieth century. It takes the 2014 Protocol to Convention No. 29, adopted at the 103rd session of the International Labour Conference, opened on May 28, 2014, for them to be formally removed from the text, nearly eighty-four years after their adoption. The protocol itself notes this in its preamble: the transitional period provided for by the convention has expired, and the articles concerned are no longer applicable. It enters into force on November 9, 2016, twelve months after the second ratification, that of Norway.

The gap between the stated principle, the prohibition of forced labor, and the legal structure of the text that carries it, a general prohibition paired with a postponement nothing forces to be shortened, sheds light on a difficulty specific to international labor law: a treaty ratified by dozens of states commits its force to the text it enshrines, not to the intention that inspired it, and a transitional clause can outlive the conditions that justified it.

repere.texte: For the purposes of this Convention the term forced or compulsory labour shall mean all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself voluntarily.
repere.source: Forced Labour Convention, 1930 (No. 29), Article 2, paragraph 1, International Labour Organization

carte.punch: The 1930 convention against forced labor itself allowed it to continue
carte.idee: Adopted by the International Labour Organization in 1930, Convention No. 29 prohibits forced labor but itself organizes a transitional period that lets the colonial powers still use it. These provisions are removed from the text only in 2014.

quiz.question: Why did Convention No. 29 of the International Labour Organization, adopted in 1930 to prohibit forced labor, itself contain provisions allowing it to continue?
choix: Because it organized a transitional period, intended notably for the colonial powers, removed from the text only in 2014
Because it applied only to countries that had not yet joined the League of Nations
Because it targeted only forced labor in the private sector, leaving public administrations free to use it
Because it provided for an automatic review every ten years, voted by simple majority of members
quiz.explication: Articles 1, paragraphs 2 and 3, and 3 to 24 of the 1930 convention organized a transitional period during which certain members could continue to use forced labor under conditions, in practice the colonial powers. These provisions were formally removed only by the 2014 protocol.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which of the following categories does the 1930 Convention No. 29 explicitly exclude from the definition of forced labor?
choix: Work done in a private business without a written contract
Prison labor carried out under public supervision
Seasonal agricultural work paid in kind
Work done by a minor with his parents' consent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 2 of the convention excludes five categories from forced labor, including prison labor carried out under public supervision, alongside military service and emergency work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does the protocol removing the transitional provisions of the 1930 convention enter into force?
choix: November 9, 2016, twelve months after the second ratification, that of Norway
June 28, 1930, the very day the convention was adopted
May 28, 2014, the day the session that adopts it opens
Immediately after its adoption, with no ratification period
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2014 protocol is adopted at the 103rd session, but it enters into force only on November 9, 2016, twelve months after the Norwegian ratification, the second one required.
